summary:
Chaco has no separate provincial statute on legal gender recognition, no provincial criminalisation provision and no provincial enforcement series in the record. A trans visitor to Chaco therefore stands under Argentina's national framework: Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval. The statute was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights, and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Protection machinery at national level has been dismantled in ways a visitor would feel. The federal anti-discrimination agency INADI has been closed, the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry eliminated, and trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota dismissed during 2024. Activists interviewed in April 2025 described the trans community's situation as chaotic and desperate, reporting worsened violence, discrimination and poverty.

Hate-crime violence is at a documented peak. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during 2025, a rise of 62% year on year and the highest count in the observatory's ten years of operation, averaging one every 38 hours; trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims (142 cases) and gay men 22% (50). The report ties the surge to institutional weakening and state legitimation of discriminatory discourse.

Judicial protection for gender-motivated violence is contested. On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, but rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.

An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration. Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010 as the first Latin American country to do so, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws.
tangentialFactors:
Chaco carries no separate reporting on trans conditions; the national record is the operative baseline for anything happening in the province.

The national pattern is one of contraction in the machinery that would otherwise respond to a visitor's complaint: the closure of INADI, the abolition of the ministry responsible for gender and diversity policy, and the dismissal of trans public-sector workers under the inclusion quota remove the ordinary points of escalation.

Comparison with the region matters here. Argentina's statute was until recently the more permissive of the Latin American gender recognition regimes, and the United Nations singled it out; the narrowing has come through decrees and administrative dismantling rather than legislative repeal, so the text of Law 26.743 remains in force while its surrounding protections have weakened.
localsOnly:
Provincial residents rely on Chaco's provincial anti-discrimination provisions alongside the national statute; the sources available here record no provincial enforcement series, no quota-compliance finding and no provincial prosecution for anti-trans violence.

Residents dismissed from public-sector employment under the labour-inclusion quota in 2024 lost a nationally administered entitlement, and the agencies that handled such complaints have been closed or abolished.

The Feb 2025 decrees on minors and on prison housing bind the province directly, since they govern access to care for adolescents and the placement of transgender detainees nationwide.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the courts have ruled on the Feb 2025 decree on minors is unresolved; the sources record the petition and the legal experts' challenge but no judgment.

No source in the inventory records any trans-specific incident, arrest, detention or complaint within Chaco itself, so the province's own enforcement picture is not sourced either way.

The relationship between provincial anti-discrimination law and national INADI's closure as it operates in Chaco is not sourced; whether a provincial body took over INADI's functions in the province is not recorded.
